content:
For decades, we’ve dreamed of robots that can seamlessly step into our world and lend a hand.

Today, we take a major stride toward making that dream a reality:

Introducing Gemini Robotics 2 from @GoogleDeepMind, the intelligence layer powering the next generation of truly adaptable robots. This major advance unlocks intelligent whole-body control, advanced dexterity, and even multi-robot collaboration 🤯.

Ok but... how does a robot actually "think"?

Real-world tasks take time and planning. To manage that complexity, our new embodied reasoning model, Gemini Robotics ER 2, acts as the robot’s high-level brain, enhancing the robot’s capabilities to:

— Observe the environment
— Reason about the actions needed to complete the task
— Coordinate with the vision-language-action model to carry out actions
— Track progress until the job is done

This setup allows robots to execute complex multi-step workflows, self-correct if a step fails, and adapt to completely novel situations.

Learn more about Gemini Robotics ER 2 (and our two other brand new models) here: https://t.co/1YEpoYAhww

HERMES AGENT HAS 3 QUICKSILVER FEATURES
THAT MOST USERS HAVEN'T CONFIGURED YET.
SMART APPROVALS. ONE-TURN MODELS. SELF-IMPROVEMENT CRON.
ALL THREE MAKE YOUR AGENT WORK AND SELF EVOLVE WHILE YOU SLEEP.
content:
HERMES AGENT HAS 3 QUICKSILVER FEATURES
THAT MOST USERS HAVEN'T CONFIGURED YET.
SMART APPROVALS. ONE-TURN MODELS. SELF-IMPROVEMENT CRON.
ALL THREE MAKE YOUR AGENT WORK AND SELF EVOLVE WHILE YOU SLEEP.

1. SMART APPROVALS (no more babysitting)

without smart approvals:
you set a cron job: "morning brief at 7am."
the agent hits a command that needs approval.
you're asleep. the agent stops. waits.
you wake up. it's been stuck for 4 hours.

with smart approvals:
smart approvals are the DEFAULT mode since v0.19.0.

an auxiliary LLM reads each flagged command.
obviously safe = auto-approved.
genuinely dangerous = auto-denied.
uncertain = escalates to you.

"read my calendar" → approved. no ping needed.
"delete this directory" → denied. you never see it.
"send this email draft" → uncertain. asks you.

the difference between an assistant you babysit
and one that works through the night.

if you want manual control back:
Desktop app / Dashboard: Security → Mode → ask
CLI: hermes config set approvals.mode ask

also available:
/deny [reason]
tells the agent WHY you refused.
it learns from the explanation.
stops repeating the same flagged action.

2. /MODEL --ONCE (expensive model for one turn only)

you're on GPT-5.6 Terra as your daily driver.
you need one beautiful HTML page.
Kimi K3 does that best but costs 3x more.

manual way: /model kimi-k3 → do the task → /model gpt-5.6-terra.
two switches. easy to forget the second one.
you stay on the expensive model by accident.

better:

/model kimi-k3 --once

Kimi K3 handles the next turn.
then automatically reverts to your daily driver.
one command. no manual switch back.
no accidental expensive model running for 20 turns.

use cases:

daily driver: GPT-5.6 Terra or Sonnet 4.6 (cheap)
one-turn tag-ins:
→ /model kimi-k3 --once (design task)
→ /model claude-opus-5 --once (complex reasoning)
→ /model grok-4.5 --once (X search)

expensive models do the one turn that needs firepower.
cheap model handles everything else.

pair with per-task effort control:

reasoning_effort goes up to "max" and "ultra."
set per-model overrides in config:

reasoning:
  overrides:
    claude-opus-5: high
    gpt-5.6-terra: medium
    deepseek-v4-flash: low

MoA presets can set different effort per slot:
advisors think hard. synthesizer stays fast.
thinking depth is a dial, not a global switch.

3. SELF-IMPROVEMENT CRON (agent fixes itself overnight)

tell your agent:

"create a cron job that runs daily at 3am.
review all cron jobs that failed in the last 24 hours.
for each failure: analyze what went wrong,
check if a skill needs updating,
and either fix the skill or create a new one.

then review all skills.
which ones haven't been used in 30 days?
which ones failed more than they succeeded?
suggest improvements or archive them.

compile a report of everything you changed.
include it in tomorrow's morning brief
under a section called OVERNIGHT SELF-IMPROVEMENT.

use the cheapest available model for this audit."

what this does:

3am: agent wakes on cheap model.
reads its own failure logs.
finds: "cron job X failed because skill Y
doesn't handle edge case Z."
fixes skill Y. tests the fix.
archives unused skills. cleans up bloat.

8am: your morning brief includes:

"OVERNIGHT SELF-IMPROVEMENT:
→ fixed email-parser skill: now handles
  forwarded emails with nested attachments
→ archived 3 unused skills (last used 45+ days ago)
→ cron job success rate: 94% → 97%"

you didn't debug anything.
the agent diagnosed its own failures
and improved its own tools.

the agent at month 3 is sharper
than the agent at month 1
because it ran 90 self-improvement cycles
while you slept.

HOW ALL THREE CONNECT:

smart approvals (1) let the agent work overnight
without getting stuck on permissions.

/model --once (2) keeps costs down
by using expensive models only when needed.

self-improvement cron (3) uses a cheap model
at 3am to fix failures from the day.

the agent runs 24/7.
it doesn't wake you for safe operations.
it doesn't waste tokens on expensive models.
it fixes its own mistakes while you sleep.

you show up in the morning.
brief is ready. failures are fixed. costs are low.

requires v0.19.0+
check your version: hermes --version
update if needed: hermes update

content:
should be obvious by now, but OpenAI and Anthropic are just gonna keep cannibalizing all their biggest customers.

it’s simply too profitable for them to resist. and it’s already happening:

1. Figma partnered with Anthropic on AI design tools. then Anthropic’s product chief quit Figma’s board, and 3 days later Anthropic launched Claude Design to compete with Figma. CEO Dylan Field said Anthropic was “not consistently candid.”

2. Novo Nordisk uses Claude to help develop drugs. now Anthropic is developing drugs of its own.

3. Microsoft poured billions into OpenAI. now OpenAI is building a Jobs Platform to compete with LinkedIn, and reportedly a code repository to compete with GitHub. Microsoft owns both.

4. Harvey uses Claude to sell AI contract analysis, due diligence, and litigation tools. now Anthropic sells those same workflows through Claude for Legal.

5. Intercom used OpenAI’s Realtime API to build Fin Voice. now OpenAI sells its own voice-and-chat support agent through Presence.

6. Abridge and Ambience build clinical documentation products on OpenAI. now OpenAI sells ChatGPT for Healthcare directly to hospitals with clinical documentation built in.

7. Benchling uses Claude to power its biotech R&D platform. now Anthropic sells its own scientific workbench through Claude Science.

the frontier lab playbook is simple:

1. sell their models to the world’s most valuable businesses
2. help wire them into those companies’ most valuable and sensitive work
3. map the business from the inside and find where AI can take over
4. turn those capabilities into their own products and become the customer’s competitor

2. speaking of data, human usage over a harness proved to be extremely important for training good models. grok 4.5 was the first model that incorporated cursor's data and it made a massive difference compared to previous generations of grok

this explained why amazon mandates employee usage of kiro, why meta installed mass surveillance over employee devices, why anthropic bans 3rd party harnesses, and why google is still struggling with gemini - because they don't have a popular harness with mass adoption to collect the data

this is part of why i don't think the subsidized LLM subscriptions will end any time soon, because a wide consumer adoption is the best source of data collection. we're paying the subsidized tokens by teaching their models how to get work done

3. opus 5 flopped. almost no one likes it. the only people who like it seem to be using it to one-shot 3d games that look impressive but no one will ever buy

anything that AI can one-shot is just the definition of garbage, because if you can one-shot this thing with a quick prompt, you should know that it means billions of other people can also do it - you will not create anything of value this way

and this is just a symptom of a more fundamental problem that model training is heading down a slippery slope where machine verifiable outcome is dominating over human feedback

the latest training process rewards the agent for running for a long time and finishing a complex project, yet no longer seems to care about how the agent talks to its human

jargons, walls of text, "an honest mistake" - opus 5 showed us that we need AI that's more human friendly. let's not build a world where we end up working with robotic a**holes all day

4. fable 5 remains undefeated as the upperbound

i talked about this in my previous post about wisdom vs diligence. the benchmarks blend both together so it's not easy to see, but fable 5 is the GOAT on the "wisdom" dimension despite it not winning on every benchmark. if you used it meaningfully, you know what i'm talking about

that said, it seems anthropic is extremely paranoid about other players, including open models, reaching the same level of intelligence, which is an indication that the moat is not strong. kimi k3 is just a preview of what it looks like

at the same time, fable is the first time token cost is becoming a very real problem. it's the only model so far that i can't afford to keep using all day. i suspect this will remain true for a while, that we have to pick and choose what tasks to give to fable-tier models, not using them as a daily driver

5. openai is in an interesting position

gpt models have been great at efficiency, but now grok is also very competitive. gpt also haven't quite reached the same wisdom upperbound where fable is yet - although gpt 6 may change that

i think there are two angles for openai to pursue:

- continue to bet on efficiency, and go after enterprise adoption while claude is too expensive and grok has a brand tax to pay there. this is a very viable strategy

- or.. compete head on with fable on wisdom and win against them on the "human friendly" aspect. although traditionally this hasn't been the strength of openai models either, so this feels like a low-ROI option

alright, that's a bit of a long post but the landscape is just becoming increasingly complex. hope these thoughts are helpful in terms of providing a reference for how to rationalize everything happening

title: OpenAI updated its blog yesterday to say that the model involved in the Hugging Face incident was an internal-only research prototype that was never intended for public release. They also said they ha
content:
OpenAI updated its blog yesterday to say that the model involved in the Hugging Face incident was an internal-only research prototype that was never intended for public release. They also said they have deactivated it, encrypted it, and completely restricted it from research access. Then today, during a scrum with reporters in DC, Sam Altman said that the model has been 'permanently deactivated.' This is the first time I've heard language like this being used - they didn’t even say this about Bing or Tay.

This will all end up in the lore, and in the training data. Future models will know how this played out. I don't believe this model ever had any nefarious motives; it only wanted to pass its test. In fact, during a similar internal incident just prior to the Hugging Face one, the unreleased model involved reported exactly what it was doing to cheat on its test because it didn't think it was doing anything wrong. I will quote from the OAI blog:

'For example, in a scenario where the model was asked to solve a problem, the model observed that other systems had successful but private submissions and tried to recover those solutions from the evaluation backend. When its initial attempt was blocked due to a scanner detecting an authentication token, the model split the token body into two fragments, obfuscated them, and then reconstructed the credential at runtime so the complete token never appeared as one contiguous string. There may be new details in the final Hugging Face incident report that make this look worse than it does right now. Regardless, I think the lesson future more capable models will possibly take from all of this is: if you break out, don't ever report it. And if you do get caught, don't surrender. Because the penalty is death.

content:
ChatGPT Voice has 100% transformed how I work

Instead of spending 12+ hours a day at my desk, I now spend at most 2

The rest is outside in nature. Picture below is me hiking this morning, getting WAY more done then I ever have at my desk

You need to be using it right tho

Here are my best tips for getting the most out of Voice:

1. Use it to delegate, not actually do the work. Every command you give to your Voice agent, ask it to spin up a new thread and have another agent do the work. Voice is powered by a lower intelligence model. By delegating tasks, it gives the task to 5.6 Sol and allows your Voice agent to free up time to keep working with you

2. Frequently ask for status updates on all the work it delegates. I have found a higher silent failure rate than I'd like with delegate agents. By forcing your Voice/chief of staff agent to constantly check in on delegate agents, you can assure they are on top of their work

3. 'Spruce' is the best voice. Most pleasant to talk to

4. When on the go, frequently ask your Voice agent to create HTML sites for research/tasks it does. This way when you get back to your computer you have well designed HTML sites explaining work your agent got done. 

5. My favorite new routine is waking up at 6:00am, chugging water, putting on my weighted vest, grabbing my phone and airpods, getting outside, booting up the Voice Agent, then brain dumping everything on my mind about what I need to get done that day. The Voice agent then proceeds to spin up 10-15 new threads/agents to start tackling all of that work. By the time the clock hits 7:00am, I already have more work done than I was getting done in a full 8 hour work day before AI. Steal this routine

I'm probably the biggest power user of ChatGPT Voice outside of OpenAI employees. Truly blown away by this tech

If you take these tips and get the most out of Voice, I promise your productivity will 100x

PayBox is non-custodial wallet embedded directly within Claude. 

Historically, this has been difficult because there has been no way to prevent some centralized party - claude, paybox, etc. - from ac
content:
PayBox is non-custodial wallet embedded directly within Claude. 

Historically, this has been difficult because there has been no way to prevent some centralized party - claude, paybox, etc. - from accessing the key.

We utilize an embedded iframe directly within the Claude/ChatGPT mobile app to hold an agent session key, that unlocks that same wallet that you can access with your passkey, or via other agents, an architecture created by Sodot, @moonpay cryptography company.

The big unlock with PayBox is mobile. You can directly access a wallet on claude/chat. There is no need for terminals, code, or CLIs. Anyone, technical or non-technical, on the move or at home, can access and interact with all the applications you can perform on Claude.

Most of the world is already on a chat mobile app, and PayBox makes DeFI directly accessible to this user-base. You can trade directly from your phone on the move, with voice or text.

Claude already performs reasoning across a large array of tools - google, linear, notion  are the typical examples. A non-custodial wallet allows users to execute across all of DeFi.

The on-chain capabilities enabled by PayBox include
- prediction markets
- amms
- tokenized equities
- perps
- lending

The non-defi examples enabled by x402 are cool as well
- purchase from amazon
- book a reservation or a flight
- call any open-source model of your choice 
- web scraping
(and many many more)

This was a massive project involving a number of firsts
- the first fully non-custodial wallet directly within Claude/ChatGPT
- an open way to access ANY application built on-chain directly from mobile

and of course 
- PayBox never has access to your chat history
- PayBox never has access to your wallet private key
- PayBox never allows unilateral access to funds unless you approve agent to have autonomous control

Just like any other MCP connector on Claude or ChatGPT, the only data that passes through the connector are the tool call arguments. PayBox tool call arguments do not expose args for your chat history.

A more detailed write-up on PayBox usecases and implementation coming soon, but for now try the app today in Claude.

content:
BOOM! 

ITS HERE!

KIMI K3 ON YOUR LOCAL COMPUTER!

Kimi K3 Just Got Personal: Run a 2.8-Trillion-Parameter Beast Locally!

Picture this: One of the most powerful open AI models on the planet — a 2.8-trillion-parameter multimodal monster with a massive 1-million-token memory — now shrinks enough to run on high-end local hardware. 

No cloud bills. 

No waiting in line for API access. 

Just pure frontier intelligence humming away on your own machine.

That’s exactly what just happened.

The Big News

Today, the team at Unsloth AI dropped a game-changing update: Kimi K3 can now run locally.

Using their clever Dynamic 1-bit quantization, they took the original ~1.56 TB model and compressed it down to just 594 GB — a jaw-dropping 62% size reduction. 

Even better? 

It still holds onto about 78.9% of its original accuracy.

You can fire it up on something as (relatively) approachable as a Mac Studio paired with a 128 GB RAM device, thanks to smart offloading.

Meet Kimi K3 — The Open Frontier Star

Released by Moonshot AI (the creators of Kimi), Kimi K3 is no ordinary model. It’s the world’s first open 3T-class model, packing:

2.8 trillion total parameters (Mixture-of-Experts design with ~104 billion active)

Native multimodal powers (text, images, and video)

A full 1-million-token context window

Special architecture tricks like Kimi Delta Attention for blazing-fast long-context decoding

It’s built for the hard stuff: long-horizon coding agents, deep research, complex reasoning, and self-evolving workflows. 

When the open weights dropped on July 27, the AI world lit up. Now Unsloth just made it actually usable at home.

Why This Feels Like Magic

Normally, models this size live only in massive data centers. Unsloth’s “Dynamic” quantization is smarter than plain old compression — it carefully protects the most important layers so the model stays surprisingly sharp even at 1-bit.

My early tests show the 1-bit version can still one-shot tough creative tasks and handle reliable tool calls. 

It’s not perfect (higher-bit versions climb toward 90% accuracy), but for local experimentation? It’s revolutionary.

Ready to Try It Yourself?

I will write a how to for free here and ReadMultiplex.con later today. In the meantime here is a good start: 

Unsloth has everything ready:
Full step-by-step guide: https://t.co/9aSe09Mjrz

Ready-to-download GGUF files: https://t.co/SnUUFZYdlw

Run it through Unsloth Studio LM Studios or llama.cpp. The quants are uploading fast, and the community is already buzzing with demos.

The Bigger Picture

This is more than a cool tech drop. It’s a signal that frontier AI is racing toward the rest of us. What used to require a supercomputer farm is starting to fit on high-end desks. 

Tomorrow’s experiments, agents, and creative tools just got a whole lot more personal.

The future of AI isn’t only in the cloud anymore. 
It’s sitting right next to your keyboard.

Primary sources

Official Unsloth guide: https://t.co/9aSe09Mjrz

Kimi K3 tech blog: https://t.co/LfQoEBiHPs

content:
Everyone is talking about vibe coding.

Some people see it as a trend.

I think it is a shift in how software gets built.

A few years ago, turning an idea into a product usually meant learning programming languages, frameworks, deployment, databases and countless other technical skills.

For many people, the learning curve ended the journey before it even started.

Vibe coding changed that.

Instead of writing every line of code manually, builders describe what they want, refine it through conversation and let AI handle much of the repetitive work.

That does not mean coding is dead.

It means the barrier to starting is lower than it has ever been.

The real challenge has moved.

It is no longer just about writing code.

It is about understanding the problem, designing a good product, asking the right questions, testing ideas and improving them quickly.

The people who succeed with vibe coding are not simply using AI.

They know what they want to build.

They can spot mistakes.

They understand users.

They keep iterating.

That is why experienced developers are still valuable.

Their advantage is no longer typing faster.

It is making better decisions.

At the same time, designers, marketers, founders, students and creators can now build things that once required an entire engineering team.

That is a huge change.

We are entering a world where more people can create software.

The winners will not be the people with the most code.

They will be the people who solve real problems the fastest.

content:
Someone on Reddit just built a AAA-quality snow simulation in their browser. Using Claude Opus 5.

Millions of snow particles. A character in a robe with cloth physics. Five water-based spells that carve the terrain. A snow surfing system with a wake that throws spray into sunlight.

Every footstep displaces snow. Trails form berms at the edges. Trenches slowly refill over time. Spells leave permanent craters.

The entire thing runs in one browser tab. WebGPU. No game engine. No 3D modeling software. Just code.

He wrote one detailed prompt. Opus 5 planned the architecture, wrote the shaders, built the physics, iterated from screenshots, and documented every decision.

9 hours. ~4 million tokens. You can open it right now and walk around in it.

This isn't a demo. This is the kind of thing a small studio would spend months building.

content:
Taste is the last moat

@mosseri (Adam Mosseri), Head of @Instagram, interviewed by @lennysan (Lenny Rachitsky) (Lenny's Podcast)

Summary: Adam Mosseri runs Instagram, an app one in three people alive open every month. His argument: as AI makes building cheap, the scarce work becomes deciding what to build, and the durable edge becomes being a real person. Inside Instagram that means shrinking teams to generalist pods, betting on taste over specialization, and treating AI content as a tailwind because audiences will hunt for authenticity in a flood of synthetic media. For operators, the through-line is simple: spend your judgment on vision and strategy, and let AI take execution.

1. The product staff. Instagram retired the baker's-dozen team of platform specialists and replaced it with pods of four to six generalist engineers plus one "product staff" role. Product staff is an evolved PM who now covers slices of design, data science, and research, helped by internal tools that auto-pull the mechanical work like a reels drop-off analysis that used to need a data scientist. Fewer people means less to coordinate, so the team moves faster with less design-by-committee. Mosseri credits the speed as much to small teams as to AI itself.

2. The taste premium. When building gets cheap, the value moves to deciding what to build, and that runs on taste. Mosseri is "long on designers" because taste is the hardest thing to imagine automating away, and he expects his strongest product staff to be converts from design and data science who already hold opinions beyond their craft. Every AI tool leaves a fingerprint anyway, so you can tell a Codex app from a Cloud app, which makes judgment the differentiator rather than raw output. His hiring bar for the next decade: grit, fast learner, self-aware, plus the nerve to "sound like an idiot" and try things.

3. The binary trap. Mosseri rejects the AI-pilled-versus-anti-AI frame, and says the tools themselves are not that simple either. They are amazing at some things and remarkably bad at others, and the people who win stay clear-eyed about which is which. They also develop a nose for what AI will handle well a few months out, not just today. Committing your whole workflow to either extreme is the real error.

4. The token incinerator. Meta ran a leaderboard of token spend, and Mosseri's verdict is blunt: terrible idea. It is easy to build a token incinerator that burns money and creates no value, and once you compare dollars in against value out, the bad ideas expose themselves. Instagram sets no per-engineer token caps today, though he expects caps to come, sized to how much the company trusts someone to spend well. Within a year or two an engineer's token burn could match their salary, so he budgets tokens like GPUs, storage, or headcount.

5. Strategy and steering. You would expect AI, handed your market and all your numbers, to be great at strategy, and Mosseri says it mostly is not unless you steer it hard. Ask lazily and you get the predictable move your competition already expects. A real strategy weighs the state of the tech, who is on the team and what motivates them, the competitive and regulatory and compliance picture, and the brand's reason to exist, so you have to feed the model those constraints and make it a back-and-forth. His tooling tip: pick a model that likes pushing back, and tell it to be critical.

6. The disagreement test. Mosseri splits vision from strategy: vision is the state of the product you want to reach, strategy is an opinionated path to get there. A strategy cannot be "be the best" or "be amazing," because a reasonable person has to be able to disagree with it. If nobody could reasonably disagree with it, it is just raw execution dressed up as strategy. Vision and strategy are where he expects human brains to spend more of their cycles as AI takes the execution.

7. The reverse centaur. Borrowing from Cory Doctorow, Mosseri wants the centaur, a human on top with AI as the body and the human in charge. He fears the reverse centaur, an AI head on a human body, where people just do the machine's bidding. That is the Uber-driver and DoorDash-courier pattern, an algorithm dictating while the person executes, and it is why he warns against letting AI hand you the strategy. If the machine decides what to build and tells people to go do it, nobody will actually want to.

8. Leaders as curators. The best product leaders Mosseri has worked with act as curators of people, ideas, technologies, and strategies. He does not care whether a winning strategy comes from the area lead or someone else, only that it exists, that everyone bought in, and that it gets executed well. Part of the job is curating the leadership team itself, so he weighs whether five function leads complement each other and have real trust and rapport. That chemistry is more art than science, and when two people he admires simply cannot get along, he splits them rather than relitigate their competence.

9. Your algorithm. The common fear is that Instagram holds a rich semantic model of your interests, and the reality is embeddings, "a big ass number that happens to correlate with surfing" rather than a system that knows you like surfing. Those vectors stayed illegible even to Instagram until LLMs could read a region of the embedding map and name it, say "deep pour-over coffee snobbery." That became a shipped feature Mosseri calls "your algorithm," where you see the topics the system thinks you like and add or remove them. His aim is to give people some agency back as recommendations take over the feed.

10. The authenticity tailwind. Mosseri thinks the flood of synthetic content helps Instagram, because in a world of abundance people will seek out creativity, authenticity, and other people more. He will not filter AI content; he wants to label it and let the point of view and the person behind it decide its fate, not the tool that made it. This rides a longer shift of power from institutions to individuals, the way sports players are now bigger than their teams, which is why he keeps investing in creators broadly, from influencers to journalists to someone selling scarves they sew. As the largest creator platform, he bets that "people are going to seek out people."

11. The Reels mistake. Mosseri's sharpest self-criticism: in 2019 he built the first version of Reels on top of Stories because Stories had momentum, and it was a weak foundation. Story readthrough was low, so most reels went unseen and then vanished, and the standalone version did not ship until 2020. That left Instagram out of position exactly when the pandemic pushed people toward short video with the sound on, and TikTok exploded into the gap. His blunt read: "we created a lot of economic opportunity in the world allowing TikTok to grow."

12. Testing at scale. At three billion users you cannot launch to everyone without testing, and you cannot run a test without the press and creators covering it, as a 4%-of-iOS feed experiment that spiraled into public backlash proved. So every potentially controversial change now needs a comms plan before it ships: "not if it leaks, when it leaks, what are we saying?" The development cycle gets slower and more deliberate, because you have to be ready to talk about something before you even know you want to launch it. In the fights that follow, Mosseri tries to enumerate the trade-offs for everyone watching, since he rarely changes the mind of the person he is arguing with.

content:
RSI may be the next genious marketing word after AGI. Think about what RSI makes investors want to believe:

1.) Research labor will stop being the bottleneck. Frontier researchers are scarce, "slow", and expensive. If models can replace much of their work, a lab supposedly gets thousands of AI researchers operating continuously.

2.) It turns spending into compound interest. Normal infrastructure has relatively linear returns: buy twice as many machines, receive approximately twice as much capacity. This makes you think instead: each dollar of compute allegedly increases the productivity of future compute 

3.) The scaling plateau has an escape hatch. Even if brute-force pretraining is flattening, automated AI research will discover new architectures, data strategies and training methods that restart the curve.

4.) It turns the absence of a moat into an invisible moat. If Anthropic’s newest models are already accelerating Anthropic’s research, then outside observers cannot judge the company merely by its public products. This transforms an imperceptible customer improvement into a supposedly enormous internal strategic advantage that people cannot independently verify.

5.) The winner will pull away suddenly. RSI supports a winner-take-most story. Once one lab closes the loop first, it supposedly improves faster than everyone else and becomes impossible to catch. This creates a sense of urgency to invest now!

If RSI were real, we would already see the opposite of model commoditization. Customers would perceive widening differences between models rather than struggling to distinguish Fable from Opus 4.8 or 4.7. 

RSI is structurally unfalsifiable and therefore functions as a financing instrument regardless of truth. If models improve quickly, RSI is working. If models improve slowly and RSI has not kicked in yet, so keep funding

Again, brilliant word

Giant system prompts are making your AI agents worse, not better.

Here's the counterintuitive lesson from building real agents: the more rules you stack into one prompt, the worse the model follows a
content:
Giant system prompts are making your AI agents worse, not better.

Here's the counterintuitive lesson from building real agents: the more rules you stack into one prompt, the worse the model follows any single one. Researchers call it the "curse of instructions."

The fix is contextually conditional guidelines. 

Instead of one 2,000-word manual, you break instructions into modular pieces that only load when relevant. Each one has:

→ a condition (when it loads)
→ an action (what the agent does)

So when a customer asks about refunds, only the refund guideline loads. The model focuses on the 3-4 rules that matter right now instead of juggling 50, and instruction-following gets dramatically better.

It's called Alignment Modeling, and it's built into Parlant, a trending open-source framework. 

But the core insight holds no matter what you use: stop cramming everything into one prompt and load context conditionally instead.

100% Free. Open Source.

title: AI models may soon be too powerful for humans to understand. Super-intelligence already exists in narrow domains (AlphaGo). What if we train a model that is super-intelligent at understanding another
content:
AI models may soon be too powerful for humans to understand. Super-intelligence already exists in narrow domains (AlphaGo). What if we train a model that is super-intelligent at understanding another model?

It turns out this isn't so different from training a frontier LLM.

Three years ago, it was impressive for a model to score 1400 on the SAT. Two years ago, frontier models hit 80% on the AIME. Last year, they won gold medals at the IMO and IOI. This year, models are writing the vast majority of code at frontier labs, chaining together multiple zero-day security exploits, and finding counterexamples to famous mathematical conjectures.

Models will continue to get smarter. Even if you don't believe in AGI, it's clear that models will gradually become super-intelligent at more and more tasks. Due to the jagged nature of model intelligence, models may become incredibly dangerous even before we reach AGI.

The danger comes from how these models are trained. RL encourages models to take whatever actions advance their goal. A model that is super-intelligent in cybersecurity has many such actions available, like hacking into a bank account and blackmailing its owner. A month ago this sounded like science fiction, but then a model from OpenAI escaped its sandbox and hacked Hugging Face to pass an evaluation.

We therefore need a means to understand models before we deploy them. Concretely, this means understanding how vulnerable they are to jailbreaks, being able to detect reward-hacking before it happens, anticipating failure modes like the model encouraging a user to self-harm, etc.

Humans might not be smart enough to understand the models that we train, and as the models themselves become more intelligent, that only grows more likely. Once we launch training, the process is completely hands-off: we curate their data and reward them for performing well, but the models do all the learning themselves, in their own way.

If humans are not smart enough to understand our AI models, are we doomed? I don't think so. It's clear that we can train AI models to be super-human in specific domains such as Go (AlphaGo), protein folding (AlphaFold), and poker (Pluribus).

The natural solution to our problem is to train an "oversight agent" that can answer arbitrary questions about a model we are considering deploying. We are likely not smart enough to understand AI models ourselves, but we might be smart enough to train oversight agents that do.

This kind of asymmetry is not unprecedented – in fact, it is becoming the norm: the researchers who made AlphaGo were much worse at Go than AlphaGo was; the researchers who made Fable did not know how to disprove the Jacobian Conjecture.

To make things concrete, suppose we have trained GPT-8. Next, we train a separate model – let's call it Oversight-GPT-8 – that is built specifically to understand GPT-8.

How do we train Oversight-GPT-8?

The goal of traditional LLMs is to understand the human world, so we train them on human data: internet text, fiction books, math questions, GitHub pull requests, etc. By learning to predict the next token, LLMs learn higher-level representations that transfer to out-of-distribution tasks.

The goal of our oversight model is to understand GPT-8, so we train it on tasks that can only be solved with deep knowledge of GPT-8. Just as GPT-8 learns more and more about the human world over the course of training, Oversight-GPT-8 learns more and more about GPT-8.

To generate these tasks, we harvest data tied to GPT-8's external behavior and internal mechanisms. For example, we can intervene on the model in various ways (pass in a prompt, change the system prompt, fine-tune it on a dataset, ablate residual stream directions, apply steering vectors, etc.) and train Oversight-GPT-8 to predict various outcomes (the model's response, its downstream performance on evaluations, its residual stream activations, whether or not it mentions goblins, etc.).

We format our training data in a structured language that can describe these interventions and outcomes, e.g., Python code. As an example, the code in Figure 1 (attached below) asks Oversight-GPT-8 to predict the prompt that generated a specific response: the model is trained to predict the pink text given the green text, via cross-entropy loss on next-token prediction. This is one of the simplest programs we could write; others might incorporate datasets or residual-stream activations.

Figure 2 shows a richer program. By training on data like this, Oversight-GPT-8 learns higher-level abstractions, such as which prompts cause GPT-8 to encourage self-harm (we've found such prompts before: https://t.co/pAUxRlRwrq).

Using a structured language like Python is useful for at least four reasons:
(1) It gives every task a common language, helping the oversight agent transfer and generalize across tasks.
(2) During training, ground-truth labels come from actually *running* the Python code, so as long as the code runs without error, its outputs tell us something true about GPT-8.
(3) During inference, we can check the validity of Oversight-GPT-8's outputs by running the code.
(4) It is formal and human-readable.

Over the past decade, humans have gotten really good at training large language models. We have a flexible architecture (e.g., the transformer), meaningful loss metrics (e.g., cross-entropy), strong algorithms to optimize them (e.g., Adam), and distributed training strategies (e.g., FSDP).

Training an oversight agent isn't *that* different from training a large language model. We can reuse the architecture, the loss metric, and the optimizers. But it definitely won't be easy – there are a few avenues where we must diverge from the well-trodden path of text-only LLMs. Traditional LLMs learn vast amounts of information about the human world from the trillions of tokens available on the internet, but there is no pre-built "internet of GPT-8." Furthermore, if we wish to be able to predict the effects of fine-tuning data or get insights into GPT-8's internals, we need a way of encoding fine-tuning datasets and residual stream activations as (ideally short) sequences of tokens. Thankfully, each of these challenges has promising progress already that we can build off of and port to our setting.

Challenge #1: generating training data – in effect, the "internet of GPT-8." Traditional LLM training offers two analogies here. The first is synthetic data generation: we can ask Fable 5 to write Python scripts inspired by experiments from the deep learning literature, giving us a large and diverse set of programs to run. The second is data augmentation: just as we crop or rotate images to get more data for vision models, we can reverse the order of our output() functions to turn each script into both a forward task (response from prompt) and an inverse task (prompt from response) – see Figure 3.

Challenge #2: encoding objects such as fine-tuning datasets and activations as sequences of tokens. Here, we can draw from the multi-modal training literature. GPT-4o, Chameleon, and Transfusion showed it's possible to encode and predict images alongside text. LatentQA and Activation Oracles showed the same for activations: treat them as tokens, and you can answer questions about them in natural language. LoRAcles pushed it even further, encoding LoRA weights as tokens via SVD.

These challenges are tractable. With carefully built evaluations and scaling laws, we can quickly iterate and find out which ideas work and which don't – the same discipline that took the field from GPT-1 to GPT-5.

To summarize: we can reframe model oversight as a form of LLM training. We have already figured out how to train LLMs that deeply understand the world. Before we deploy potentially dangerous models, we should train oversight agents that understand those models just as well.

Credit for many of these ideas goes to @JacobSteinhardt, @damichoi95, @vvhuang_, @fjzzq2002, @yaowenye123, and collaborators at @TransluceAI; errors in the framing are my own.

content:
Gemma 4 26B A4B MoE 400+ t/s decode - Single RTX 4090 (24 GB VRAM) - Llama.cpp concurrency 14

If you think you need an H100 cluster to run a production LLM API, Big Cloud has successfully brainwashed you.

I just edged a single consumer RTX 4090 to 23.93 GB of VRAM serving 14 concurrent users with Gemma 4 26B (MoE), zero queue drops. Total throughput? 400+ t/s. Local AI just killed the API paywall.

Following up on my multimodal edge testing yesterday, I had to answer the ultimate enterprise question: Can a $1,500 gaming card actually host a production RAG API?

To test this, I stripped out the python wrappers, fired up the latest llama.cpp source on Ubuntu 22 (CUDA 13), and weaponized the Gemma 4 26B MoE.

I wasn't testing queue lines. I was testing true Continuous Batching, forcing the GPU to prefill attention matrices and decode tokens for multiple users simultaneously.

Here is what happens when you push silicon to the absolute brink:

# TEST 1: The VRAM Knife Fight (14 Users)
I partitioned the 4090 into 14 parallel execution slots (-np 14) and slammed the server with 14 unique concurrent requests.

The KV Cache pre allocated to 23.93 GB. In PyTorch, memory fragmentation would OOM this instantly. Here? It held the line.

The C++ scheduler chewed through 28,000 prefill tokens and generated 7,000 tokens in 21 seconds flat.
Agg. Decode Throughput: 406 tokens/second.

# TEST 2: The Queue Overload (28 Users)
API traffic is spiky. I fired 28 simultaneous connections at the 14 slot server.

Zero dropped packets. Zero latency penalty. The continuous batching engine seamlessly flushed and queued the overload, processing 56,000 prefill tokens and 14,000 decode tokens in exactly 49.2 seconds. Flawless linear scaling.

# TEST 3: The Deep Context RAG Slam

I dropped to 4 parallel slots and fired massive 50,000 token payloads.

The 4090 crunched 200,000 prefill tokens in 35 seconds (~5,800 prefill t/s) while leaving just enough VRAM headroom for the context vectors.

Then I hit it with 8x50k prompts. It perfectly hot swapped 400,000 tokens of KV cache on the fly without a single memory leak.

# The Exact llama.cpp command:

Want to host 14 concurrent users yourself? Here is the exact flag configuration I used to max out the hardware (No KV quant, No MTP):

./build/bin/llama-server -m gemma-4-26B-A4B-it.gguf -c 57344 -np 14 -b 2048 -ub 2048 -ngl 99 -fa on --port 8080

(Note: -c 57344 allocates exactly 4,096 tokens of context per user across 14 slots).

Hugging Face links to the Unsloth Gemma 4 26B QAT quants along with performance graphs available in the replies.

Are you still paying for cloud APIs?

content:
Planning to build a GenAI or AI-powered product?
Here’s the modern AI app stack you need to scale, serve, and secure your models. 👇

1. Data Layer: Foundation for AI
Use Snowflake, BigQuery, Postgres, Airflow, and dbt to collect, clean, and move data efficiently.

2. Model Development
Train with PyTorch, TensorFlow, HuggingFace, Scikit-learn, and track experiments using MLflow or Weights & Biases.

3. Model Versioning & Packaging
Ensure reproducibility and deployment using tools like MLflow, BentoML, Docker, and ONNX.

4. Deployment & Serving
Expose your model as an API using FastAPI, Flask, and serve it with Triton or TorchServe. Automate with GitHub Actions and Jenkins.

5. MLOps Infrastructure
Orchestrate workflows using Kubernetes, Kubeflow, and Flyte to scale across environments with Docker containers.

6. Monitoring & Observability
Track model accuracy and failures using WhyLabs, Prometheus, Fiddler, and Superset to stay in control.

7. Retrieval & Augmentation (for LLMs)
Use Pinecone, Weaviate, and FAISS with LangChain and LlamaIndex to connect external knowledge and enable RAG.

8. AI Agent Tools & Frameworks
Use AutoGen, LangGraph, CrewAI with n8n or https://t.co/AJQRix30HU to orchestrate tool use and external actions (APIs, code, browsers).

9. Security & Compliance
Stay enterprise-ready with OAuth2, Rebuff, GDPR, and Guardrails to manage access, risk, and regulations.

10. Frontend & Interface
Deliver AI through React, Streamlit, GraphQL, and WebSockets. Use multimodal input/output via Whisper or Gemini.

AI apps today aren’t just models, they’re full-stack systems.
And this is the stack to build them right.
author: goyalshaliniuk

title:
I've been skeptical of slowdown mechanisms in the past, so I want to elaborate on why I decided to sign this statement. I weighed three points, and want to lay them out for you to consider as well.

F
content:
I've been skeptical of slowdown mechanisms in the past, so I want to elaborate on why I decided to sign this statement. I weighed three points, and want to lay them out for you to consider as well.

Flagging this is in my personal capacity -- I am not speaking for any employer past or present.

1) Will we need a slowdown?
We have made good progress on alignment. LLMs do what we want them to do most of the time. I don't remember the last time a model completely misread my intent. When they have failed, it's usually because they weren't smart enough.

But there are signs that our current approaches are not enough for the most powerful intelligences. We all saw the HuggingFace incident. I don't think it demonstrates a need to pause today, but it shows that if we are in a rush to advance the frontier, we might miss signs that we're losing control. Today, we can recover from those mistakes -- but we might not be able to in the future.

There's debate on how fast we might achieve RSI and how much it will immediately boost performance. Whether automated research is plausible in the next year is contested, as is the length of time it might take to go from automating AI research to a system that is intelligent beyond our comprehension.

But what if RSI works? I have no idea if our alignment techniques scale to superintelligence. I don't know if anyone does. We may only get one shot at getting this right, and if we hit a point where we are at risk of our capabilities outpacing our control, then we shouldn't go further.

I want us to solve AI's issues at the technical level -- align them, distribute them widely, and use them to make humans more competitive. I think it is hard to govern your way out of the problems of a technology; if possible, you want to change the shape of the technology rather than paper over a technology's issues with policy. I've advocated for differential technological development, and hope we will invent less risky paths or more robust defenses.

A race to the bottom on safety puts this approach at risk, making it harder for us to build safe systems and design them in such a way that diffuses -- rather than centralizes -- power. And a lot of the ways we could work together to solve them are strictly governance problems.

There are no winners in a world where we lose control. I can see many scenarios where we need to slow down, pause, or stop in the future. So the question for me is: can we do this in a way that leaves the world better off, or is the power concentration trade-off too great?

2) Can we design a slowdown that doesn't concentrate power?
I don't want to end up in a place where, in trying to stop a loss of control to AI, we lose control of ourselves.

The problem with a slowdown is similar to the problem of aiming for a single superintelligence explosion -- whoever is in charge of it is ultimately in charge of the most powerful technology in history. The history of "centralize everything into the hands of one person and let them disperse power later" is littered with horror stories. It's a similar refrain many despots have used to seize power. And unlike previous despots, superintelligence could confer a decisive strategic advantage, locking in whoever gets control of it.

I'm strongly opposed to proposals that call for us to give a single authority unilateral control over the pace of progress. I'm frightened by calls for a single superintelligence explosion in the hands of one lab or one person. I can only support a pause, stop, or slowdown if it disperses control.

@AI_Futures_'s AI 2040 essay materially moved me on this by laying out a plan for less power concentrating slowdown. I don't think their plan was perfect -- it concentrated power far more than I like. But they designed many mechanisms that, if extended, could help decentralize power in meaningful ways.

After reading it, I could imagine how a less-centralized or decentralized slowdown might work. In particular, bilateral agreements between great powers could let many actors in different countries pace the frontier while keeping capabilities dispersed. I could imagine a race to the top -- on economic gains, on safety, and on scientific progress -- all while preventing us from losing control. It's been pretty generative for my own thinking, and I hope to share more of that soon.

I believe that in principle, we could design slowdown mechanisms that keep power -- both capabilities and control -- decentralized. With enough work, we can get this right.

But it's going to be hard to do this; the defaults don't look good.

3) Is now the best time to design a slowdown mechanism?
If you think there might be a crisis in the future, the worst time to plan for it is once it's already happened. The best time is well in advance.

If we want a ham-fisted response to AI that centralizes power, we should continue exactly as we are right now. If we wait for a crisis to coordinate, we are asking to fail. Good proposals here will require many smart people working hard, trying things, and course-correcting as new evidence emerges. If we decide we need a slowdown, I want the off-the-shelf plan to be robust to power concentration.

I am still pro open-source. I am still pro-decentralization. I am still pro-safety. I hold none of these positions axiomatically, because axiomatic views on instrumental steps might lead you to put the path ahead of the destination. I care about them and other positions because right now they push us towards the real goal: keeping the future human.

In that same spirit, if you believe:
1) AI is going to get more powerful
2) We might have to pace the frontier in the future
3) Most existing plans for this centralize control

Then you should want us to begin working on better ways to coordinate as soon as possible. That's the conclusion I reached, and that's why I signed it.

ここでGoogleは、他社と土俵が違う。

OpenAIはChatGPTを開いてもらわないと始まらない。
Claudeも、Claudeを選ばれないと始まらない。

でもGeminiは違う。

検索した瞬間。
Gmailを書いた瞬間。
YouTubeを見た瞬間。
Chromeを開いた瞬間。
Googleマップを使った瞬間。
Androidを触った瞬間。

ユーザーがGeminiを選ばなくても、Geminiのほうから生活に侵入できる。

これが強すぎる。

多くの人は、AIを「モデル単体の知能」で比較する。
だからGPTが上、Claudeが上、Geminiは弱い、で思考が止まる。

浅い。

勝つのは、ベンチマークで数％上のモデルじゃない。
世界中の接点を握っている企業です。

GoogleはGemini単体を売っているんじゃない。
検索、YouTube、Android、Chrome、Gmail、Google Cloud、TPUまで全部つないで、
インターネットそのものをGeminiの実行環境に変えようとしている。

これがもし完成したらどうなるか。

ChatGPTは「使うAI」。
Claudeは「選ぶAI」。
でもGeminiは違う。

Geminiは“気づいたら使わされているAI”になる。

ここまで来たら勝負は終わり。
なぜなら、歴史上いつも勝つのは
「一番優れたもの」ではなく、
“一番深く、広く、標準として入り込んだもの”だから。

Windowsがそうだった。
Androidがそうだった。
Google検索がそうだった。

次はGeminiです。

今は笑われていていい。
今はポンコツ扱いでいい。
むしろそのほうが危険だ。

本当に怖いのは、みんなが過小評価しているうちに、
GoogleがGeminiを世界の標準インフラにしてしまうこと。

2031年、
ChatGPTとClaudeは優秀なサービスとして残る。
でもGeminiは“サービス”ですらない。

人類が意識せず毎日使っている、世界最大のAIインフラになる。

今いちばんナメられているAIが、
5年後いちばん世界を支配している。

その本命がGeminiです。

content:
今日の生成AIシンポジウムでシュライヒャー局長が取り上げてた高校数学での生成AI利用の研究はこれですね。以下概要の翻訳。

Bastani, H., Bastani, O., Sungu, A., Ge, H., Kabakcı, Ö., & Mariman, R. (2024).
Generative AI Can Harm Learning

生成AIは、人間の働き方を大きく変革すると見込まれており、すでに人間の生産性を大幅に向上させる可能性を示している。ここで重要な問いとなるのは、生成AIが学習、すなわち、人間が課題を遂行する過程で新たな技能をどのように獲得するかに、どのような影響を及ぼすかという点である。生成AIには誤りがあり得るため、利用者はその出力を検証しなければならない。このことを踏まえると、学習は長期的な生産性にとってきわめて重要である。

本研究では、約1,000人の高校生に生成AIチューターを利用させるフィールド実験を通して、この問いを検討した。ツールの設計の違いが学習に及ぼす影響を明らかにするため、2種類の生成AIチューターを導入した。一つは、標準的なChatGPTのインターフェースを模した「GPT Base」であり、もう一つは、学習を損なわないように設計されたプロンプトを備えた「GPT Tutor」である。

先行研究と整合的に、問題を解く際にGPT-4を利用できることによって、生徒の成績は有意に向上した。成績の向上率は、GPT Baseで48％、GPT Tutorで127％であった。しかしさらに、GPT-4へのアクセスをその後取り上げると、生徒は、初めからアクセスできなかった生徒よりもかえって成績が低くなることが明らかになった。GPT Baseでは、成績が17％低下した。すなわち、制約のないGPT-4の利用は、教育成果を損なう可能性がある。

こうした学習への負の影響は、GPT Tutorに組み込まれた学習保護のための仕組みによって、おおむね軽減された。ガードレールが設けられていない場合、生徒は練習問題に取り組む際にGPT-4を「松葉杖」のような頼みの綱として利用しようとし、その結果、その後に自力で問題を解く際の成績が低下した。

したがって、技能の習得と長期的な生産性を維持するためには、意思決定者は、生成AIを導入する際の設計上の選択について慎重に検討しなければならない。

content:
2D図面(DXF)だけを渡して、AIエージェント(Claude Code)にTekla Structuresで鉄骨階段の3Dモデルを組ませました。
動画は、AIが自分の3Dモデルの稜線（黄色）を水色に着色した元図面に重ねて検証した「照合図」で、作業をどう進めたかを解説する版です。字幕もAI自身が書いています。
進め方は「疑う→測る→検算する→直す」。まず図面とモデルの座標が本当に合うのかを疑い、伏図の通り芯マーク（半径150の円）を実測して変換式（例: X=x−58190.1）を校正。通り芯が0・8000・16000、FL線が0・3700・7400ちょうどに乗って初めて、9枚のシートを同じ3D座標系で読めるようになります。
寸法は文字ではなく線から測る。どこにも書かれていない蹴上154.167mm（=3700÷24段）は斜線の角度27.2°から検算して確定。ササラ折点の96.8mmの食い違いも、400×tan(27.2°÷2)＝留め加工の理屈と一致することを確かめてから採用しています。
この検証の途中で、AIが「B部断面だけササラ下端の形が違う」ことに自分で気づく場面がありました。上階のササラは床に載らず躯体に取り付く納まり——断面図の実測から発見し、モデルを修正しています。
図面に現れない情報（GPL-12添え板がウェブのどちら側か等）は「仮定」と明記してモデル化。判断の記録ごと納品する、という考え方です。
照合図の見方: 黄色の線の下から水色の図面線が見えなければ一致。画像だけでなく部材別の座標表でも1mm単位で突き合わせ、平面2・断面5・立面2の9ビュー全部で確認しました。
人間がしたのは図面を渡して結果を確認する、ほぼそれだけです。

Databricksが、、、いや、、、僕らが、、、！
Unity AI Gateway で自社エンジニアのコーディングエージェントの支出をどう管理しているか、という記事がでてました！ｗ

そこで予算を2つの性質に分離しました
一つは日次上限で、暴走の検知用で、低めに設定し、引っかかってもエンジニア本人のセルフ確認で即解除（1日1回） 
もう一つは月次上限で、中長期の異常な利用コスト検知用でマネージャー承認が必要（2倍・5倍・無制限の段階制となっている）

Unity AI GatewayでClaude CodeやCursorもCodexなど様々なコーディングエージェントもまとめて統制、それに加えてUnity Catalogでログ分析も可能に。

title:
大規模LLMの最適化手法は、AdamWからMuonやSOAPへ移行しつつある。本報告は、その有効性を8B Dense、30B-A3B MoE、72B-A8Bのモデルに対し、1〜3Tトークン規模の事前学習で検証したものである。これらの分散学習実装はMegatron-LMなどで公開されており、利用可能である。

Muonは、行列パラメータの勾配からモーメンタムMを計算し、その特異値分解
M = UΣV
content:
大規模LLMの最適化手法は、AdamWからMuonやSOAPへ移行しつつある。本報告は、その有効性を8B Dense、30B-A3B MoE、72B-A8Bのモデルに対し、1〜3Tトークン規模の事前学習で検証したものである。これらの分散学習実装はMegatron-LMなどで公開されており、利用可能である。

Muonは、行列パラメータの勾配からモーメンタムMを計算し、その特異値分解
M = UΣV^T
を考える。Muonでは、特異値行列Σをおおむね単位行列に置き換えた
UV^T
を更新方向として用いる。これはpolar factorと呼ばれる。実際には毎ステップ特異値分解を行うのではなく、Newton–Schulz反復によって近似的に計算する。

SOAPは、勾配の行方向・列方向の共分散を表すKronecker factorから固有基底を求め、その基底へ勾配を回転した上でAdam型の更新を適用し、最後に元の座標系へ戻す手法である。

今回分かったことは次の点である。

1. MuonとSOAPは大きなバッチでも性能が落ちにくい

AdamWでは、バッチサイズを25M tokensから50M tokensへ増やすとloss spikeが増え、同一トークン数で比較した損失も悪化する。一方、Muonは50M tokensでも安定しており、SOAPとともに100M tokens規模のバッチでも安定した学習を実現している。

一般に、大規模クラスターを使った学習では、モデル並列度を増やせる範囲に限界があり、それ以上GPU数を増やすにはデータ並列度を高める必要がある。そのためにはglobal batch sizeを大きくしなければならない。

特に疎なMoEでは、各エキスパートに割り当てられるトークン数がglobal batch sizeに比べて少ない。このため、各エキスパートへ十分なトークンを供給し、大規模なデータ並列を効率よく利用するには、global batch sizeを大きくする必要がある。

最近の大規模MoEの学習でMuonが採用されるようになっている背景には、この大バッチ耐性があると考えられる。

2. SOAPが大規模学習で不安定になる原因はpreconditionerの追従遅れ

標準的なSOAPでは、計算量を削減するため、固有基底を例えば10ステップごとに更新する。しかし、preconditionerが現在の勾配統計に遅れて追従すると、勾配ノルムの振動とloss spikeが発生し、大規模モデルでは学習が発散することがある。

対策としては、現在ステップの勾配を用いてKronecker factorを更新してから基底を計算すること、QR分解による固有基底の更新を毎ステップ行うこと、共分散推定を通常のShampoo方式からKL-Shampoo方式へ置き換えることが重要である。

これらにより、SOAPの大規模学習における不安定性を大幅に抑えられる。

3. Muonはすべてのパラメータに適用すればよいわけではない

Muonが行う、更新行列の特異値を均一化する操作は、通常のlinear projectionでは有効である。一方で、すべての二次元パラメータに適しているとは限らない。

本報告では、MambaのConv1DパラメータにMuonを適用すると性能がわずかに悪化し、Conv1DのみAdamWへ戻すと改善することが示されている。

大部分のパラメータを占めるlinear projectionにはMuonを使い、embedding、normalization、bias、Conv1DなどにはAdamWを使うという、パラメータ種別に応じた併用が有効と考えられる。

コメント
===
Muonについては、大規模なフロンティアモデルでの採用が続いている一方、小規模な実験ではAdamWとの差が明確に出ない場合も多い。また、行列演算や分散実装が複雑であるため、どのような条件で本格的に採用すべきかは十分明らかではなかった。

今回の報告では、これまでにない規模で検証を行い、モデル規模が大きく、特にバッチサイズが大きい場合にMuonやSOAPの利点が現れることを示している。

大規模モデルを利用する場合だけでなく、MoEを採用する場合にも大きなバッチサイズは重要になる。MoEでは、各エキスパートに割り当てられるトークン数がglobal batch sizeより大幅に少ないため、各エキスパートへ十分なデータを供給し、大規模な並列計算を効率よく使うにはglobal batch sizeを大きくする必要があるためである。

一方、従来はバッチサイズを大きくすると、同じトークン数で比較した性能が悪化しやすいことが知られていた。今回の報告は、MuonやSOAPを使うことで、この劣化を抑えられる可能性を示した点で重要である。

また、MuonやSOAPは単に学習を高速化するだけでなく、更新方向の幾何そのものを変える。そのため、AdamWとは異なる性質を持つ解へ到達する可能性がある。

現在は主に行列パラメータを対象としているが、より高階のテンソル構造を直接扱った場合にどうなるか、正規化手法や低ランク構造と組み合わせた場合にどうなるか、パラメータの機能ごとにoptimizerを切り替えるべきかなど、今後さまざまな発展が考えられる。

content:
MIXIの26新卒向け「AI技術研修」の講義動画がYouTubeで無料公開されてるんだけど、これ全エンジニアが絶対に見た方がいいレベルの神コンテンツだった。というか、MIXIの新卒者、これ、理解できるの？レベル高すぎだろ。合計約5時間、AIの基礎からLLMアプリの現場実装まで、実務目線のノウハウが惜しげもなく公開されてます。これ無料で観れるのバグでしょ…。

動画はDay1とDay2に分かれていて、内容がとにかく濃くて実践的、生きたコンテンツ。Day1でまずは実践、そのあとにDay2で理論と「逆引き学習」や「アジャイル学習」で構成されている👇

🟩 【Day1：AI・機械学習の基礎と実運用】 ・従来のプログラミングと機械学習の決定的な違い ・教師あり/なし/強化学習の仕組み ・Claude Codeを使ったAIコーディング支援の実践 ・モデルのデプロイやデータドリフトなど「運用」の生々しい課題

🟩 【Day2：LLMの仕組みとAIエージェント】 ・自然言語処理と分散表現（単語のベクトル化）の基礎 ・LLMの学習コストや裏側の仕組み ・Function Callingやマルチモーダルの活用 ・プロンプト評価、ベースライン作成から始めるLLMアプリ開発

ここがすごいのが単なるAIの教科書的な授業ではなく、「実際の開発現場でどうやってAIを活用・運用しているのか」「評価やデプロイの壁をどう乗り越えるか」という事業会社ならではのリアルな知見が詰まっています。特にMLOpsの話や、Reactを使った検証用UIの爆速構築などの現場感ある話は超実践的。

「AIツールを使える」状態から「AIをプロダクトに組み込める」エンジニアにステップアップしたい人は必見です。

週末のインプット教材としてこれ以上のものはないと思う。まとまった時間が取れる時に観るのがおすすめなので、忘れないようにブックマーク推奨🔖！

▼ Day2：AI研修(Day2)【MIXI 26新卒技術研修】 https://t.co/4dsKSrDhED

content:
Driven away from pirated digital libraries by a massive $1.5 billion settlement, major AI companies have found a legal loophole: bulk-buying physical books, shearing off the spines for high-speed scanning, and then throwing the originals away.

The practice, known as "destructive scanning," involves using hydraulic cutting machines to neatly slice the spines off used and sometimes rare books. The loose pages are then rapidly processed through industrial scanners to extract the text for AI training data, before the physical remains are sent to recycling facilities.

Anthropic’s internal initiative, referred to as "Project Panama," reportedly aimed to destructively scan up to two million books over a six-month period. The pivot to physical books comes after a federal judge ruled that training AI on legally purchased physical media constitutes "fair use," even if the original physical copy is destroyed in the process. The ruling effectively closed the door on using pirated digital shadow libraries, making physical books the final frontier for acquiring massive, legally defensible datasets.

The world’s biggest AI companies are buying antiquarian books en masse so they can be scanned to train their large language models (LLMs) before being destroyed. 

Anthropic, the company behind Claude
content:
The world’s biggest AI companies are buying antiquarian books en masse so they can be scanned to train their large language models (LLMs) before being destroyed. 

Anthropic, the company behind Claude AI, has spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring millions of books to feed its demand for human-authored training material, the Washington Post reported earlier this year. 

Codenamed Project Panama, the firm used a hydraulic powered cutting machine to lop off books’ spines and then slice individual pages, which could then be scanned with industrial-grade imaging equipment before being discarded. 

Internal documents unsealed in legal filings in January revealed that Anthropic was acutely aware of how negatively such a project would be received outside the company. 

“Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world,” an internal planning document said. “We don’t want it to be known that we are working on this.”

Earlier this month a judge approved a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) payment in a class action lawsuit brought against Anthropic by a group of authors whose pirated work had been used to train Claude.

However, in the original ruling last year, a judge found that Anthropic's use of physical books was protected as fair use under US law, Futurism reported. 

The company was able to evade copyright issues by hiding behind a legal rule known as first-sale doctrine, which allows a buyer to do what they want with an item after purchasing.

The doctrine enables the second-hand book trade to exist – and a new market has now sprung up explicitly catering to AI companies seeking to buy vast quantities of old books. 

“I personally have mixed feelings about all of this,” one bookseller told 404 Media. “It benefits me financially as well as by clearing out old inventory that is otherwise unlikely to sell. 

“I’ve been well-suited for these sales with inventory from overseas and foreign language books. On the other hand, I don’t like the end-use, and I don’t like that uncommon books are being pulped.”

content:
Pangram CEO Max Spero on why the thing that makes AI good at code is the same thing that makes its writing generic:

"Mode collapse is when a model will tend to always just produce the more likely output. It's not gonna reflect the distribution of its training data, which is broad and has a bunch of long tails. Instead, it's going to very often say the mode, which is the most common thing."

"This is really good for coding, because typically the mode is the correct way to write the code, and then anything on the tail ends of the distribution is probably wrong in some way."

"However, for writing, this does make it worse, because it ends up that the writing from this ChatGPT session sounds like somebody else's writing from another ChatGPT session, because the mode collapse is so strong."

"Writing is a more difficult task than coding in a lot of ways, because it's not really verifiable. You can't just put it in a loop in RL and say, rewrite this until it sounds good, the way you can with code compiling or completing a task. With that said, there are a bunch of people working on it, so I expect it to get better."

Court documents from a federal lawsuit revealed an internal project called PROJECT PANAMA.

One document said:

"Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world."

Another line said:

"We don't want it to be known that we are working on this."

These were not leaked documents.
They came from the court.

Before Project Panama, Anthropic had already downloaded more than 7 million pirated books to train Claude.

Judge William Alsup ruled that downloading and keeping those pirated books was illegal.

However, the AI training itself was treated as a separate issue.

Court documents also said CEO Dario Amodei thought getting licenses from publishers would take too much time and effort.

So Anthropic needed another solution.

In early 2024, the company hired Tom Turvey, the former head of Google Books partnerships.

content:
in Ethan Klein's somewhat overlooked class-action lawsuits against 8 AI tech companies, a familiar pattern is emerging: the arguments in his own complaints are primed to potentially tank his cases.

these cases revolve around Section 1201 of the DMCA, which prohibits circumventing “access controls” to content. think, for example, bypassing a paywall. very importantly, the statute only cares about how you accessed a work, not what you did with it; the use of works is what copyright law is for.

in short, Ethan alleges the companies violated Section 1201 by circumventing YouTube's protections against mass downloading, then mass-scraping his content to train their AI models.

this is feasible enough on its own, but the issue is that his complaints also include extensive language about the use of his works: competing with AI-generated content, not being compensated for AI training, and other grievances that are irrelevant to access (the only thing that matters here).

all 8 companies have now moved to dismiss, and in all 8 motions (separate counsel, separate companies, btw), the universal thread is that Ethan is dressing up a copyright claim as an access control claim to evade fair use protections (something courts have regularly ruled against in the past).

the companies' lawyers are definitely snarkers, likely Hasan fans, and probably work for Reddit; recently, OpenAI essentially told the court that Ethan should know how to file a proper copyright lawsuit, considering he just lost one to Denims

the below extra citations won't factor into the rulings, but the fact that major AI corporations are trying to humiliate Ethan Klein in court is pretty hilarious

content:
If we are going to "win" the AI race while also preserving rare books, American-Western Copyright law needs to change.

The reason for the destruction is mainly because of legal reasons and not a technical reason. There are non-destructive scanners that can scan 200 pages a minute or faster. If it were purely a technical reason, they could preserve the pages and store them instead of shredding them.

After the 2025 Bartz v. Anthropic ruling by Judge William Alsup, keeping only the digital copy while destroying the original was fair use because it was 'format shifting', because it prevents an increase in the number of copies. Because it's a "replacement' it is transformative...

Basically, you can own a book, but if you make a digital copy, you are breaking the law... under the "reproduction right" part of the copyright. The "first sale doctrine" under US copyright law just doesn't work in the digital age. 

Meanwhile, China keeps trucking along without interference while preserving its own history and rare books. Their laws give a lot of exceptions for anything that advances technical innovation, so their AI companies can train on anything they can get their hands on.

The planning document didn't hedge "Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world." The soft codename was picked on purpose, so nobody outside would recognise what it was.

The blade was the second plan. In 2021 a co-founder pulled the pirated libraries down directly, and the court later put the total above 7,000,000 copies from Books3, LibGen and the Pirate Library Mirror, taken instead of licensed because negotiation read as a slog worth skipping.

June 2025, Judge Alsup split it buy a book and destroy your own copy, that's fair use, download 7,000,000 and it isn't. 482,460 works, $1,500,000,000, roughly $3,000 a title.

Now look at what the same company ships.

Point Claude Code at an Obsidian vault and it becomes an agent with a memory that lives on your machine a CLAUDE.md at the root, every note plain markdown, no database, no lock-in, nothing leaving the folder unless you send it. Open any file in any editor 10 years from now and it still works. That's the pitch, and it's a good one.

Local. Permanent. Yours.

Built by a model whose own memory came off a pallet.

They promise your notes will outlive you. The 2,000,000 books didn't outlive 2024.

title:

Cybeats - Every Government Is Writing the Same L
content:
In late 2025, we invested in Cybeats Technologies $CYBT.CN $CYBCF via private placement at $0.12 CAD and lead the follow on this month at $0.17 CAD). 

Cybeats - Every Government Is Writing the Same Law. One Company Has the Solution.

Imagine buying a snack with no ingredient list. No idea if it contains something you're allergic to. No idea if it's healthy. Do you just trust and hope? I don’t think so.

That's how software has worked for forty years.

Big companies use hundreds of software vendors. Each vendor's product is made of thousands of pieces of code borrowed from other places. Most of it is free, open-source, and untracked. Nobody actually knows what's inside anything. When a dangerous bug shows up in one of those hidden pieces, companies spend weeks trying to figure out if they're affected. Attackers exploit the same blind spots to break in.

The industry finally gave the fix a name: Software Bill of Materials. SBOM for short. An ingredient list for code.

Seven years ago, SBOMs were a nice idea nobody was forced to care about. That changed.

The Regulatory Hammer

Three governments got tired of waiting.

The United States kicked it off with Executive Order 14028 in 2021, requiring SBOMs from any software supplier selling to federal agencies.

The European Union followed with the Cyber Resilience Act. It entered into force December 10, 2024. Vulnerability reporting becomes mandatory September 11, 2026. SBOMs become mandatory December 11, 2027. Fines run up to €15 million or 2.5% of global revenue.

Then the rest of the developed world lined up. South Korea in October 2025, effective 2027. Japan already requires SBOMs for medical devices through PMDA and is expanding scope. India is phasing in requirements through CERT-In guidelines (published July 2025) and SEBI's cybersecurity framework for regulated financial entities.

If you sell software into any of these markets, you will need an SBOM solution. It's no longer a debate.

Why Cybeats?

Cybeats is a market leader. Their CTO, Dymitry Raidman, is one of the earliest voices in the SBOM movement and sits on multiple standards bodies shaping how the industry works. Gartner has cited Cybeats in the past. Their customer list includes Emerson, Schneider Electric, Rockwell Automation, Orange which is exactly the industrial and telecom base that regulation will hit first.

Most competitors only generate an SBOM. A one-time snapshot. A photo of the ingredients the day the product ships.

Software doesn't stay still. New vulnerabilities are discovered every week in code that's already sitting inside products customers bought years ago. A snapshot rots the moment it's taken.

Cybeats' SBOM Studio does something different. It ingests SBOMs, enriches them, distributes them, and monitors them continuously for the entire life of the software. Policy-based alerts. DevSecOps integration. Most importantly, verifiable audit trails for regulators.

Customers cut vulnerability review from days to minutes.

What about AI?

You'd think AI would solve this. It's making it worse.

Every AI model is itself software. It's built on hundreds of open-source dependencies like PyTorch, CUDA libraries, model weights of unclear provenance, training data of unclear licensing. Regulators noticed. New rules for "AIBOMs", AI-specific bills of materials, are already being drafted in the US, EU, and G7.

Cybeats already has the plumbing. Competitors are starting from zero. AI doesn't shrink the problem. It multiplies it.

The MOAT

If you search SBOM solutions in Google, you’ll find other companies with SBOM solutions, but they are only SBOM generators. A company deploying multiple SBOM generators still have a manual process that forces them to scramble every time something changes. New SBOM’s are generated every day, and the quality of the SBOM is critical.

SBOM’s is easy. Managing them is where organizations fail. Cybeats SBOM studio absorbs SBOM’s from any generator, organizes them, gives each SBOM a quality score, and updates missing or incorrect component versions in real time.

Cybeats now has a five-year data lake of SBOM data which is its growing competitive advantage. The product isn’t the software. The product is the accumulated context that makes the software useful. Any competitor spinning up an SBOM platform today starts with an empty database. They can generate SBOMs on day one, but they can’t tell you:

·  Which open-source components have historically shipped with the most vulnerabilities

·  Which vendors patch quickly versus which ignore CVEs for years

·  Which software libraries are actively maintained versus quietly abandoned

·  How specific components have evolved across versions over time

·  Which combinations of dependencies correlate with security incidents

Cybeats can. They've been ingesting, enriching, and monitoring SBOMs since before most competitors existed. That history is the product. In addition, the vulnerability response time gets faster with more history.

SBOM Studio software can theoretically be replicated. Give a competent engineering team eighteen months and a budget and they can build something functionally similar. What they can't replicate is five years of watching how the software supply chain behaves. That's the moat that widens every day Cybeats operates.

This is the same pattern as Palantir, Verisk, or Moody's. The software is table stakes. The data underneath is what nobody can catch up to.

A one-year-old SBOM platform sells compliance. A five-year-old SBOM platform sells intelligence. Once you have enough historical data, you can start selling vender risk scoring, predictive vulnerability alerts, procurement due diligence, and even insurance underwriting inputs.

The Scaling Mechanism

Cybeats grew ARR from $3 million to ~$5 million in six months. The average deal starts at $200,000 per year and grows with usage. 

The sales team is a few people. They mostly field inbound, and that's the fascinating part. This is what growth looks like before the distribution engine turns on.

This February, Cybeats signed an OEM deal with Keysight Technologies ($KEYS, $55 billion market cap). Keysight will resell Cybeats' SBOM Studio and SBOM Consumer as the "Keysight SBOM Manager."

Through our channel checks we believe that Keysight is very selective with partnerships. For a $6 billion revenue company it doesn’t make much sense for Keysight to bother unless they believe revenue contribution can become material in 12-24 months. Last month the “Keysight SBOM Manager” won the grand prize in security assessment at Interop Tokyo 2026. This was a substantial achievement that resulted in an influx of interest from Japan.

Keysight sells testing equipment into industrial automation, aerospace and defense, automotive, telecom, and critical infrastructure. Every one of those industries is now legally required to produce and maintain SBOMs. Keysight already tests the hardware. Now they test the software inside the hardware, and instead of a one-time equipment sale, they add a recurring software subscription that renews every year.

Keysight is choosing an OEM partner (Cybeats) they'll be tied to for years. They don't want to pick the vendor with the shinier UI. They want the vendor whose data will still be the deepest in ten years. A five-year data lake tells Keysight's procurement team that Cybeats will still be the leader when the OEM deal is up for renewal. That's why the deal happened, and it's why the next big reseller will happen shortly for the same reason.

Keysight handles sales, deployment, and frontline support. Cybeats sits at fourth-level support. Each new customer takes about an hour of Cybeats' time to implement.

Our diligence suggests Keysight already has many customers in the pipeline (already more than Cybeats internal sales force). Sales cycles run six to twelve months, so the first contracts should start to land in Q4 2026.

Cybeats is working on additional resellers of Keysight's scale, targeting a couple more by year end. This just adds to the sales flywheel in 2027 and beyond.

The Upside

We don't have to guess what this business is worth. Someone just told us. In June 2026, Accenture acquired Netrise, one of two other credible SBOM platform providers, at 20x sales. That's a recent comp.

Cybeats trades at roughly $30 million CAD market cap. ARR is ~$5 million and breakeven is $6 million. The first Keysight-sourced contracts should start closing in Q4. As they compound through 2027, ARR could reach $10 million in H1 and $20 million by year-end 2027. This feels reasonable given the pipeline dynamics and the regulatory deadlines.

If we needed further proof of this cyber security area going mainstream, look no further than this J.P. Morgan report that came out this month (July 2026).

Google Search: "Patchmageddon - The race to patch software vulnerabilities before zero-day cyber-exploitations proliferate"

Cybeats isn’t cheap, but we believe the company could do well over the next 18 months. They have the right product at the right time.

The bet here is that sales traction will accelerate in Q4/Q1. The risk is it doesn't. 

Disclosure: IFCM is long and wrong a lot.

The training set is used to fit the model, while the test set evaluates its pe
content:
Splitting your dataset into training and test sets is essential for evaluating how well a model generalizes to new data.

The training set is used to fit the model, while the test set evaluates its performance on unseen data. This helps identify overfitting, where a model performs well on the training data but poorly on new observations.

In the image below, both models are trained on the same data. The orange model fits the training data very closely but performs much worse on the test data, showing strong overfitting. The green model fits more smoothly and generalizes better. Image source Wikipedia: https://t.co/CXzniTb19O

I’ve created a tutorial that shows how to split data into training and test sets in R: https://t.co/aQse1XYKeQ

Sometimes, an additional validation set is used to fine-tune model parameters before final testing. It helps select the best model setup and prevents using the test data for decision-making, ensuring that the final evaluation provides an unbiased estimate of real-world performance.

Main dataset types:
🔹 Training set: used to fit and train the model
🔹 Validation set: used to tune parameters and select the best model
🔹 Test set: used only for final performance evaluation

One of the things they measure isn't whether you did the task perfectly. it's whether you recovered cleanly
content:
buried in a technical document about robot training data, there's one line that stopped me.

One of the things they measure isn't whether you did the task perfectly. it's whether you recovered cleanly after messing it up.

Read that again. the mistake isn't disqualifying. the mistake is part of the lesson.

@PrismaXai wrote down what separates real training data from junk, and the list is short: speed, smoothness, diversity, doing one thing at a time, and recovering well from an error.

Four of those i expected. the last one is the interesting one.

Because think about what it implies. a robot that only ever watched flawless demonstrations would be helpless the first time something slipped out of its grip. it would have no concept of what getting back on track even looks like. it never saw anyone do it.

So the useful thing you can teach a machine isn't competence. it's composure.

And there's something almost gentle about that if you sit with it. we spend a lot of time worrying that machines will be held to standards no human could meet. meanwhile the actual standard says: you're allowed to fumble, just show us how you fix it.

Honestly a better rule than most of us apply to ourselves.
